title: tsdb [PERF]: optimize head ShardedPostings with shard bucket postings
body:
`ShardedPostings` on head previously filtered by doing a `stripeSeries.getByID` lookup for every input posting so it could read the cached shard hash. On large heads this makes query sharding pay a per-series map lookup once per shard for every queried postings list.

This PR adds a head shard bucket postings index. When sharding is enabled, each series is inserted into a bucket derived from its stable shard hash. For power-of-two shard counts, `ShardedPostings` intersects the input postings with the relevant bucket postings instead of resolving every series through `getByID`.

The bucket index preserves the existing modulo-sharding contract:
- Power-of-two shard counts use the bucket index.
- Power-of-two shard counts larger than the bucket count use the matching bucket, then lazily resolve the intersected candidate refs for the final shard-hash filter.
- Non-power-of-two shard counts fall back to the generic per-series filtering path.
- The bucket index can be disabled with `ShardedPostingsBuckets < 0`, while keeping sharding enabled through the generic fallback.

This also adds the optional reader-scoped `ShardedAllPostingsReader` interface for callers that need all head postings for a shard, plus `HeadOptions.ShardedPostingsBuckets` and `Options.ShardedPostingsBuckets` so embedders can tune or disable the bucket index.

Dirty bucket repairs replace full bucket slices. Churn-heavy embedders can opt into a bounded `ShardedPostingsBufferRecycler` and share it across DBs or Heads through `Options` or `HeadOptions`. Displaced buffers become reusable only after every index reader that could still observe them closes. Retention is bounded by the configured byte budget and 128 idle buffers; constructing the recycler with a zero budget disables it. Head repair counters and recycler hit, miss, eviction, rejection, retained, and pending-retirement metrics make the allocation rate and retained memory observable.

The implementation keeps bucket refs sorted for efficient intersection. Normal series creation appends in order; out-of-order appends mark the affected suffix dirty. On read, a copied bucket is sorted in full if the dirty region begins before the midpoint; otherwise only the necessary suffix is sorted. Candidate buckets are captured independently, and returned postings remain valid after unlock for their index reader's lifetime because existing slice contents are not mutated. A separate per-bucket replacement mutex serializes sorting and removal without blocking clean readers or appends. Dirty sorting and survivor rebuilding prepare replacement slices outside the main bucket lock, carry over concurrent append tails, and briefly re-lock to install the result. Deleted series carry their shard hash into bucket removal, so GC rebuilds only affected buckets.

Bucket entries are ref-only. Earlier experiments stored an aligned shard-hash sidecar for over-bucket shard counts, but that added measurable creation-path overhead. The current implementation keeps the cheap exact bucket path and handles over-bucket shard counts by intersecting first, then doing lazy shard-hash lookups only over the reduced candidate set.

Bucket-backed `ShardedPostings` routes through `index.Intersect`. Earlier experiments compared this against a custom sequential shard-filter strategy, and `index.Intersect` won across shard counts `{2,4,8,16,64,128,256}` for both flat and merge-tree inputs.

#### Benchmarks

Environment: `darwin/arm64`, Apple M4 Pro. Comparisons used `go test -benchmem -count=6`. Benchmarked comparison base: `prometheus/main` `7070104b3485ae8999d6e77f9c654df4af42b1d6`; main-equivalent benchmarked branch revision: `6b8979e47d9dd7213dec7ff089e8b94362a896ce`. The baseline was `prometheus/main` patched only with the benchmark harness used for this comparison so both sides exposed the same benchmark names. Remove-path and branch-only diagnostic measurements were captured at `3cb990234ce81bb10648f2b453e9e624d34ab565`, except for the fallback all-postings comparison refreshed at `f3dead9ceb09d7625852b461b9cb9f35f140938a`. The current branch head is `148e128f00780c81ea9e25f16a8f9a167c83362e`; it retains the bucket-routing query path and adds reader-scoped `ShardedAllPostings` plus opt-in repair-buffer recycling. The main-equivalent tables remain revision-pinned evidence for the bucket-index query path, while the remove-path table is explicitly historical and the current lock-contention and recycling measurements are summarized below.

Benchmark names were reorganized after these measurements. Historical benchstat output remains verbatim; current names map as follows:

- `ShardBucketDirtySort` -> `ShardBucketPostings_DirtySort`
- `ShardBucketPostingsFootprint` -> `ShardBucketPostings_Footprint`
- `ShardBucketPostings/add` -> `ShardBucketPostings_Add`
- `ShardBucketPostings/shardPostings` -> `ShardBucketPostings_PostingsFor`
- `ShardBucketPostings/remove` -> `ShardBucketPostings_Remove`

The comparison below measures intermediate revision `3cb990234` against its parent `cb6589826`, when survivor rebuilding first moved outside the main bucket lock. It remains evidence for moving the linear survivor scan and allocation out of that lock, but predates the current replacement mutex and independent bucket-capture design. The current head keeps survivor rebuilding outside the main lock, serializes slice replacements separately, and has no stale-snapshot fallback that rebuilds under the main lock.

Dense shardCount=16 remained bound by each read's own eight-bucket merge. Pure removal throughput was unchanged to slightly improved, with unchanged removal allocations. Survivor slices reserved 16 refs of append headroom (capbytes/live 8.16 vs 8.00). title: storage: add in-memory native RW2 metric metadata
body:
Depends on #19457.

## Why

Remote Write 2.0 carries metric type, unit, and help per series, but the receiver can currently store that metadata only through the experimental legacy WAL-backed metadata path. This draft adds an independent native TSDB path so that RW2 ingestion, metadata changes over time, and API exposure can be reviewed separately from persistent storage.

Keeping this prototype in memory is intentional: it narrows the first step to the ingestion and query contracts while leaving WAL and block persistence for a follow-up.

## What changes

- Add the experimental `--enable-feature=native-metadata` flag.
- Pass RW2 metadata through `AppenderV2` and retain timestamped, per-series
  type, unit, and help versions in the Head.
- Bound histories to 32 versions per series and report both history and result
  truncation.
- Expose the data through the experimental `/api/v1/metadata/series` endpoint,
  with series matchers and a result limit.
- Keep the existing `metadata-wal-records` path independent.

The API's category and version envelope leaves room for additional native metadata categories and persistent backends without coupling this prototype to a particular persistence format.

## Non-goals

- WAL, checkpoint, snapshot, block, or Parquet persistence.
- Metadata ingestion from scrapes, OTLP, Remote Write 1.0, or Agent mode.
- Replacing or removing the existing `metadata-wal-records` feature.

#### Which issue(s) does the PR fix:

Part of #12608.

Related to #15911.

```release-notes
[FEATURE] Remote write: Add experimental in-memory storage and API exposure for Remote Write 2.0 metric metadata behind the `native-metadata` feature flag
```

title: Scrape configuration to limit label churn / added series
body:
## Problem: Cannot limit per-instance or per-job label _churn_ over time

Prometheus presently supports limiting the number of distinct series that may be scraped for an instance in a single scrape, with the `sample_limit` scrape setting. This effectively limits the permitted `scrape_samples_post_metric_relabeling` for an instance (with some [caveats](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/16427) around scrape cache size, label rewrite cache size, and staleness marker handling).

But there is no meaningful way to limit the number of series a workload may create _over time_. A rogue workload that emits series with rapidly changing labels can add a huge number of series to the TSDB. This has a similar impact on TSDB index sizes and Prometheus query memory use to a workload that emits an excessively wide data set in a single scrape.

Excess label churn can be _monitored_ using `sum_over_time(scrape_series_added{...}[$duration])`, possibly with a threshold computed from `scrape_samples_post_metric_relabeling` to ignore some amount of absolute  label churn that represents low percentage churn in jobs with very high overall series counts. But there's not currently any way to make a Prometheus instance _actively robust_ such that it automatically defends against excessive churn.

## Proposal: Enforce scrape-time limit on `scrape_series_added`

Ideally Prometheus would have a way to limit the label or series churn a workload can introduce to the TSDB.

### Option 1: Threshold on `scrape_series_added` with a first-scrape exception

Ideally Prometheus would have a way to limit the `scrape_series_added` of a workload.

```
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "somejob"
    # ...
    sample_limit: 100
    series_added_limit: 5      # discard new series once scrape_series_added > 5 for this scrape
                               # and report in a new scrape_series_discarded{limit="series_added"}

```

A simplistic limit would be useless since new instances would be adding only new series, so they'd immediately hit the limit. So enforcement of the limit could be skipped if there are no recent samples for this `up{job, instance}` in the TSDB, probably defining "recent" as within 2 configured scrape-intervals for this job.

### Option 2: Limit the sum of scrape_series_added over a time window

Instead of a first-scrape exception, the churn limit could be expressed as a limit on new series added over a time window.

In this case the limit would be applied for new series introduced by the instance over some configured duration, dropping new series added once the threshold defined by `sum_over_time(scrape_series_added{job="$job",instance="$instance"}[$duration])` ) over the specified duration is reached.


```
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "somejob"
    # ...
    sample_limit: 100
    # Discard new series if the rolling sum of
    # scrape_series_added{job,instance}[$duration] would
    # exceed the configured limit.
    series_added_over_time_limit: 200
    series_added_over_time_limit_duration: 1h
```

With this approach the `series_added_over_time_limit` would have to be >= the `sample_limit` or scrapes of new jobs would fail. So to be useful, the duration over which the churn limit is to be computed must be fairly long, since a problem "rogue" job may only be rapidly churning a small subset of its series.

## Limitations

This proposal would help with label churn over time, but would not limit all sources of excessive memory use. Notably:

> [[...] metrics dropped via metric_relabel_rules are still cached](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/12443)

and of course there's no memory quota on queries so queries can use potentially unbounded memory.

Being able to limit label churn would still be a significant step toward making Prometheus more robust without as much hands-on tuning and management.

## Possible implementation issues for discussion

### Requires appender to query the TSDB

The first approach would require the appender to query the TSDB HEAD to determine whether a past scrape for this instance has occurred, in order to decide whether to enforce the new series limit.

If the 2nd approach of a limit over time was taken, the appender would have to query the TSDB for the sum of `scrape_series_appended` over the limit-interval. This query might reach the most recent non-HEAD block during periods soon after a HEAD block roll-over.

In either case, the queries could have a nontrivial cost and latency.

### Difficult to implement in agent mode

Both approaches would presumably be unsuitable for Prometheus running in agent-mode since it has no true TSDB and no querying capabilities. It is unclear how an agent-mode Prometheus could meaningfully apply label churn limits. But a scrape-time churn limiting approach would also presumably be ineffective for series ingested via a Remote Write push. So it's unclear how a target label churn limit could be enforced when using a hub and spoke deployment of Prometheus instances in agent mode.

A simple per-instance in-memory cache with an array of time-bucketed counters might offer an alternative to querying the TSDB. But then enforcement of the limit would temporarily cease to be effective after any Prometheus restart, potentially allowing bursts of high-churn series to be ingested from problem workloads. And the extra per-instance memory consumed for bookkeeping might be nontrivial.

### Would not defend against churn from restarting workloads

This configuration won't defend Prometheus against churn from a workload that restarts rapidly, causing new series to be scraped each time.

A `Job`-level limit would possibly be useful for this, or some separate limit on number of instances over time (rather than just number of currently active instances as is currently supported).

## Related

* https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/16427
* https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/11372
* https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/16620
* https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/455
* https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/12443#issuecomment-2820069060

title: [RW2]: Prometheus client_golang remote API adoption
body:
### Proposal

Adopt the https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang/tree/main/exp/api/remote from client_golang to replace the current custom remote write handler implementation in Prometheus.

### Context

This proposal is part of the broader https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/16944 outlined in PROM-35. The current Prometheus implementation in storage/remote maintains its own custom protocol handling logic for both v1 and v2 remote write protocols. Meanwhile, the Prometheus team has built an official remote write client in client_golang that does the same thing but is designed to be shared across the ecosystem.


### Benefits

Using the official client means we can share the same remote write implementation with other projects like Mimir, Thanos, and Cortex. It also means protocol updates happen in one place instead of being scattered across different codebases. 

### Potential Concerns

The main concern is that the exp/api/remote package is marked "experimental." However, this refers to the API potentially changing, not the protocol stability. The Remote Write protocol itself is stable - the experimental label just gives flexibility to refine the API before it's locked in (with Prometheus as the core user).

We'd also want to coordinate this with other PRW2.0 work to avoid conflicts.

title: Feature Request: Add Labelmap PromQL Function
body:
# Summary

Add a PromQL function for labelmap available during querying with a similar behavior to the `labelmap` action in the relabel config.


# Explanation

Currently, PromQL supports the `label_replace()` function, which is an incredibly useful function in manipulating labels during querying for compatibility reasons and to allow for better aggregation.

With that said, there is currently no way to preform that renaming for a group of labels. The `label_replace()` requires a source label and a destination label - meaning it is bound to a single replacement.

In the case where multiple replacements are needed, the only available solution is to nest these functions one within the other. Apart from increasing the complexity of the query and reducing readability, this approach fails when the labels we wish to manipulate are not fixed or dynamic. 

Currently, there is **no way** to manipulate **a changing set of labels** at the querying level.

# Solution

Prometheus already offers a great solution to a nearly identical problem during relabeling: the `labelmap` action.

We propose to add a PromQL function which acts exactly like the relabel action.

Note that this idea is a somewhat mix between the classic `labelmap` action and the `label_replace()` function.

This approach is simple, and in-short, copies the `labelmap` action behavior to a usable PromQL function. It syntax goes as follows:

`labelmap(query, regex, replacement)`

1. `query` defines the PromQL query being manipulated.

2. `regex` defines the **label name** of the labels being manipulated. Only labels matching said regex are affected. 

3. `replacement` defines the new **label name** used for each affected label. Supports regex capture groups.

### Example:

Assume the following PromQL query:
`up{job="kubernetes_pods"}`

Returns the following series:

`up{job="kubernetes_pods", kubernetes_cluster="cluster1", kubernetes_namespace="namespace1", kubernetes_pod="pod1"}`

`up{job="kubernetes_pods", kubernetes_cluster="cluster2", kubernetes_namespace="namespace2", kubernetes_pod="pod2"}`

`up{job="kubernetes_pods", kubernetes_cluster="cluster3", kubernetes_namespace="namespace3", kubernetes_pod="pod3"}`

Notice many of the label names start with `kubernetes`. For this example, we'd want to drop that prefix from all relevant labels.

Disclaimer: although this is possible to do permanently during relabeling, saving it like that is not always desired and irreversible - unlike a PromQL function, which is relevant only for a specific query.

If we surround our query with the new `labelmap` function as follows:

`labelmap(up{job="kubernetes_pods"},"kubernetes_(.+)", "$1")`

We get as a result the following:

`up{job="kubernetes_pods", cluster="cluster1", namespace="namespace1", pod="pod1"}`

`up{job="kubernetes_pods", cluster="cluster2", namespace="namespace2", pod="pod2"}`

`up{job="kubernetes_pods", cluster="cluster3", namespace="namespace3", pod="pod3"}`

Notice how the `job` label is unaffected.

This way, we achieve an almost identical behavior to the relabel action, while preserving the flexibility a PromQL function offers.

# Benefits

1. The best of both worlds: add supports for dynamic “label renaming” that the `labelmap` action offers while preserving the flexibility the `label_replace()` function has.
2. Familiar concept: simple and relies on existing behavior.
3. Offers a solution for a use case currently unavailable when querying.

We would love to hear more thoughts on the matter, and hope (if eligible) to see it implemented in the near future!

title: prombench: Is Prombench reliable enough? fix or document ignorable baseline
body: > NOTE: Prombench is implemented mostly in [test-infra](https://github.com/prometheus/test-infra) repo, but adding issue here for visibility, as we make decisions based on prombench in this repo. Prombench is relatively unreliable. With [the recent proposed updates to the dashboard](https://github.com/prometheus/test-infra/pull/937) that shows and the average percentages of the difference across core metrics it yields extra +/-~3% allocs/s, +/-~6% CPU use, +/-3% HTTP latency The unreliability yields wasted time on chasing non-existing issues (e.g. https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/18022), or it masks existing issues. What's funny, it tends to be the "PR" node that is mostly worse for some reasons (order of creation?) Perhaps it's the effect of exact average calculations vs the YOLO "it looks kind of good to me" look on a graph, and it was always there, but in this issue I'd like to see what we can do to either: * Understand and improve reliability (especially on CPU side) * If we can't improve, document and improve dashboards to show the typical variance and when (how long to wait) e.g. make the numbers white if within acceptable ranges. Some tips on what we see from profile are [here](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/18022#issuecomment-3861807883) and it suggests kernel page behavior with mmaps, but it's a long shot. ### Ideas A) To rule out accidental use of irrelevant commits, I propose we extend prombench start logic to always build both PRs from source by default: https://github.com/prometheus/test-infra/pull/940 B) Find current variance baseline and document, I can update dashboard PR for i C) Investigate deeper e.g. * Load we put to both * Run PMU (e.g. https://github.com/perfgo/perfgo) to understand what happens with the process that gets worse (e.g. on cache misses). ### Evidences I ran exact 1:1 Prometheus's via custom prombench scenario: https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/18036#issuecomment-3870073553 Both using `quay.io/prometheus/prometheus:{{ .RELEASE }}` From what I looked so far, the load on both Prometheus-es are equal (queries, samples/s) Yet the variance is clear

title: Support periodic DNS re-resolution for FQDN targets discovered via Consul SD
body:
### Proposal

In dynamic environments where services are accessed via FQDN (e.g., multi-tenant systems behind nginx), IP addresses frequently change due to instance rescheduling or migration.

In our setup, Prometheus uses Consul service discovery and targets are defined via FQDN. When the underlying IP changes, Prometheus does not re-resolve DNS for already discovered targets. As a result, targets become permanently DOWN even though they are healthy and reachable.

This behavior creates a significant operational issue:

- Monitoring becomes unreliable
- Alerts are triggered incorrectly
- Manual intervention is required to recover

We verified that:

- DNS updates correctly reflect new IPs
- Prometheus only re-resolves DNS when the target is rediscovered (e.g., after deregistration and ~6 minutes delay)
- Restarting Prometheus also restores correct behavior, as DNS is resolved again on startup

This demonstrates that DNS resolution is tied to discovery events and process lifecycle, rather than ongoing scraping.

In environments where IPs are ephemeral and FQDN is the only stable identifier, this limitation makes Prometheus difficult to operate reliably without additional workarounds.

title: Deltas: add PromQL function to disable processing of start times
body:
We anticipate that some exporters will generate bad start times, and users may need a way to ignore those start times on a per-query basis.  While the preferred solution to bad data is fixing the bad data, this could appear as breakage for users if queries used to work and suddenly don't when they enable start time processing. We want to give them an option short of having to leave start time processing disabled globally, so a new function seems to be a good approach.

Such a function could be called something like `ignore_start_times()` or `drop_st()` and would essentially return the contained series as-is, but with all start times removed.  (This will require design: do we want them to be NaN, or zero, or empty slice of STs?)

Please do not volunteer for this issue, it is for internal tracking and will be assigned.

title: scrape: allow setting multiple URL parameter values via __param_ labels
body:
#### Which issue(s) does the PR fix:
Fixes #18348

#### What this PR does
A `__param_<name>` target label carries a single string, so a URL query parameter that
takes a list of values (e.g. `match[]` when federating) cannot be fully configured via
service discovery or relabeling; only the first value can be set.

This adds `__param_<name>_<i>` labels, where `<i>` is the zero-based position of the
value (a decimal integer >= 1 without leading zeros):

- The value replaces the configured value at position `<i>` if it exists, otherwise it
  is appended.
- Indexed labels are applied after the bare `__param_<name>` label, in ascending numeric
  order of `<i>` (`_2` before `_10`).
- Any other suffix (`_0`, `_01`, `_x`, trailing `_`) is not special and names the
  parameter literally, so existing behaviour is unchanged. The only new collision is a
  parameter whose own name ends in `_<i>`; this is documented.

Example, from a file_sd target:
```yaml
labels:
  __param_match[]: '{job="node"}'
  __param_match[]_1: '{job="prometheus"}'
```
produces `?match[]={job="node"}&match[]={job="prometheus"}`.

Bare `__param_<name>` semantics, `PopulateDiscoveredLabels` (which still exposes only the
first value) and the config schema are untouched. No feature flag is added since behaviour
only changes for label names matching `__param_<name>_<i>`; happy to gate it if preferred.

Changes:
- `scrape/target.go`: parse indexed `__param_` labels in `Target.URL()`.
- `scrape/target_test.go`, `scrape/scrape_test.go`: table cases for override, append,
  gaps, numeric ordering, invalid suffixes and the end-to-end scrape request.
- `docs/configuration/configuration.md`: document the indexed form.

#### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered).
*Reviewers should verify clarity and quality.*

```release-notes
[ENHANCEMENT] Scrape: Allow setting multiple values of a URL query parameter via `__param_<name>_<i>` target labels.
```

title: discovery/kubernetes: re-resolve targets on node updates for nodeName-only addresses; deflake UpdatedNodeMetadata tests
body:
#### Which issue(s) does the PR fix:

Fixes #16387

#### What this PR does:

Investigating the flaky `TestEndpointsSlicesDiscoveryWithUpdatedNodeMetadata` turned up a production bug as the underlying cause, plus two test-infrastructure races. All three are fixed here.

**Production bug — node updates don't re-resolve nodeName-only addresses.** The endpoints and endpointslice node indexes ([`kubernetes.go`](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/discovery/kubernetes/kubernetes.go)) only recorded nodes referenced through a `TargetRef` of kind `Pod` or `Node`. An address that carries a bare `nodeName` without a `TargetRef` — which is exactly what `buildEndpoints`/`buildEndpointSlice` attach node metadata for — was never indexed, so `enqueueNode` found nothing on a node update and the targets kept stale node labels until an unrelated event re-resolved them. Reproducible deterministically: with the tests below expecting the post-update label, the endpoints variant times out forever because the update never propagates. Both indexes now record every node the target builders may attach metadata for (the address's own `nodeName`, `Node`-kind TargetRefs, and not-ready addresses, which also get node labels).

**Why the test was flaky (both directions):**

1. The two `*WithUpdatedNodeMetadata` tests asserted the **pre-update** node label, so they passed only when the update failed to propagate within the 1s collection window and failed when it did (the flake in the issue). They now assert the post-update label, matching their names and intent.
2. The fake clientset delivers events only to already-registered watchers, and an informer reports `HasSynced` after its initial LIST but before its WATCH is registered — an update issued in that window is lost forever (a real API server replays it via `resourceVersion`). The tests now wait for the node watch registration (via a `PrependWatchReactor` signal) before mutating the node.
3. `readResultWithTimeout` could only stop early by reaching a distinct-source count that single-source tests can never reach, so they always rode the full 1s window and asserted whatever state happened to be last. It now also stops as soon as the merged result equals the expected one, making the final-state assertion deterministic and independent of the window size (raised to 10s purely as a safety net for slow runners — matching tests exit immediately, both fixed tests now complete in ~0.2s instead of >1s).

Verified: `go test ./discovery/kubernetes/ -run UpdatedNodeMetadata -count=5` deterministic green, full package green.

#### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered).
*Reviewers should verify clarity and quality.*

```release-notes
[BUGFIX] Kubernetes SD: With `attach_metadata.node` enabled, node label updates now propagate to endpoints and endpointslice targets whose address references its node only via `nodeName` (no `targetRef`); previously such targets kept stale node metadata until an unrelated update.
```

title: `kubernetes_sd_config`: support retrieving K8s deployment/cronjob/job name
body:
### Proposal

In order to better correlate Prometheus and OpenTelemetry metrics, we would like adopt the OpenTelemetry naming specifications ([link](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/blob/main/docs/non-normative/k8s-attributes.md)) on Prometheus metrics.
This requires to discover the name of the deployment/cronjob/job that create pods so in addition to supporting `__meta_kubernetes_pod_name` in `kubernetes_sd_config`, we would like to have `__meta_kubernetes_deployment_name`, `__meta_kubernetes_conjob_name`, and `__meta_kubernetes_job_name`.
This feature seems to be implemented in the [OpenTelemetry Collector K8s Attributes Processor](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/tree/main/processor/k8sattributesprocessor) navigating from the pod description to the controlling daemonset/statefulset/replicaset and again navigating to the controlling deployment/cronjob/job.

For feature parity with Openelemetry, the Prometheus discovery could also add support for discovering the daemonset/statefulset/replicaset.

title: Duplicate Scraping Issue with EndpointSlice Role Using ipFamilyPolicy=PreferDualStack

title: rules: migrate rule evaluation to AppenderV2
body:
Part of #17632. **Stacked on top of #19455** (mandatory, batched `AppendExemplars`) — base branch is `krajo/appenderv2-mandatory-exemplars`.

TL;DR: trivial switch of rule evaluations to AppenderV2, due to having no metadata or exemplars or indeed start timestamps.

## What

Rule evaluation (`rules/group.go`) and stale-series cleanup are ported from V1 `storage.Appender` to `storage.AppenderV2`:

- `ManagerOptions.Appendable storage.Appendable` becomes `AppendableV2 storage.AppendableV2`.
- Both `g.opts.Appendable.Appender(ctx)` call sites (`Eval`, `cleanupStaleSeries`) become `g.opts.AppendableV2.AppenderV2(ctx)`.
- The `AppendHistogram` / `Append` / `SetOptions` trio collapses into the unified `Append(ref, ls, st, t, v, h, fh, opts)` call. `AppenderV2` has no `SetOptions` — options are passed per call — so `g.appOpts` changes from `*storage.AppendOptions{DiscardOutOfOrder: true}` to `storage.AOptions{RejectOutOfOrder: true}` and is passed directly on every `Append` call (sample results, histogram results, and stale markers) instead of being set once on the appender.

### Incidental behaviour fix

In the old code, `SetOptions` was only called immediately before the plain-float `Append` branch, never before `AppendHistogram`. Since `SetOptions` mutates shared appender state, a histogram result only got `DiscardOutOfOrder` if a float result happened to be processed first in the same evaluation; a rule group returning only histograms got none. Passing `g.appOpts` explicitly on every `Append` call (float, histogram, and stale marker alike) makes this consistent regardless of sample type or order.

## Wiring

- `cmd/prometheus/main.go`: `Appendable: fanoutStorage` → `AppendableV2: fanoutStorage` (already implements it).
- `cmd/promtool/unittest.go`: `Appendable: suite.Storage()` → `AppendableV2: suite.Storage()` (already implements it via `promqltest`).

## Tests

`rules/manager_test.go` and `web/api/v1/api_test.go` just rename the field — no mock changes needed, since `teststorage.TestStorage` and `promqltest.LoadedStorage` already implement `AppenderV2` by embedding `*tsdb.DB`.

title: otlptranslator: keep le="+Inf" equal to count when a bound is +Inf
body:
The OTel Go SDK accepts `+Inf` as an explicit bucket boundary: `AggregationExplicitBucketHistogram.err()` validates only
that the boundaries are monotonic, so `Boundaries{1, 2, math.Inf(1)}` is accepted, and recording through it emits
`explicit_bounds = [1 2 +Inf]` with `bucket_counts = [5 2 3 0]`. The trailing bucket spans `(+Inf, +infinity)`, so it
cannot hold an observation.

On input of that shape this path emits `le="+Inf"` twice for the same series and timestamp: once from the loop over
explicit bounds, carrying the running sum at that bound, and once synthesized from `pt.Count()`. Both samples are
written. The two values are equal whenever `count` equals the sum of the bucket counts below the bound, which the
producible shape satisfies, so the defect there is the duplicate write alone; they diverge only when the data point
violates the sum rule as well, either through a non-empty trailing bucket or a `count` that is not the sum of
`bucket_counts`.

The change skips an infinite bound in the loop, lets the synthesized bucket carry the count, and reports the bound:

```go
if math.IsInf(bound, 1) {
	c.plusInfAnnots.Add(newCategorizedWarningf(WarningCategoryHistogramPlusInfBound,
		"histogram data point has an explicit +Inf bound, le=\"+Inf\" is taken from count"))
	continue
}
```

`explicit_bounds` is required to be strictly increasing, so `+Inf` is the last bound and no later bucket depends on the
skipped iteration; its own count is already added to the running sum before the guard. The bound's exemplars still reach
the synthesized bucket through the remainder assigned after the loop, so no exemplar is dropped. No pre-existing fixture
in the package set an infinite bound, so the guard changes no output that was already covered.

The NHCB path already refuses this input: `checkHistogramCustomBounds` rejects an explicitly defined `+Inf` bound in
`model/histogram/generic.go`, reached from `Histogram.Validate`, and #17320 kept that while relaxing `-Inf`. Repairing it
silently here was inconsistent with that, hence the warning, in the same category style as
`histogram_zero_count_non_zero_sum`. It is merged into the annotations `FromMetrics` returns, and deduplicated by
message, so a translation reports it once however many data points carry the bound.

`TestPrometheusConverter_AddHistogramDataPoints` covers three shapes: the one a producer emits, and two that are invalid
in different ways, a non-empty trailing bucket and a `count` above the bucket sum. All three fail without the guard.

#### Which issue(s) does the PR fix:

Fixes #19424

#### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered).
*Reviewers should verify clarity and quality.*

```release-notes
[BUGFIX] OTLP: Do not emit `le="+Inf"` twice when a histogram's explicit bounds end at `+Inf`, and warn about the bound.
```

title: otlptranslator: make the histogram_1 test fixture OTLP-conforming
body:
`TestFromMetrics`'s `histogram_1` fixture sets `count` to 15 with `bucket_counts` of `{3, 11, 0}`, which sum to 14. OTLP
requires the two to agree, and the native-histogram expectation the test asserts inherits the mismatch — handed to
`histogram.Validate`, that expected value is refused:

```
14 observations found in buckets, but the Count field is 15: histogram's observation count should equal the number of observations found in the buckets (in absence of NaN)
```

The declared `sum` of 155 settles which side is wrong: 14 observations at or below the last bound of 1.123 cannot sum to
more than 15.8, so at least one observation belongs in the `(1.123, +Inf]` overflow bucket. The first commit sets that
bucket to 1. It is not emitted as a `_bucket` series, so the classic expectations are unchanged; only the
native-histogram delta moves, from `-11` to `-10`.

The second commit checks the property instead of the number: every expected native histogram in that block goes through
`Validate` before the comparison, so an expectation the appender would reject fails the test. Reverting the first commit
while keeping the second makes `TestFromMetrics/successful/convertHistogramsToNHCB=true` fail.

The check is scoped to that block. `TestTemporality`'s expectations come from an exponential data point with `count=1`
and no buckets, which is a question about that input rather than about the expectation.

title: scrape: reject zstd responses when the feature flag is off
body:
`readResponse` matches `Content-Encoding: zstd` and then uses `break` to skip decompression when the `zstd-scrape` feature flag is disabled. `break` only leaves the `switch`, so `reader` stays `resp.Body`, the raw zstd frame is copied into the scrape buffer and handed to the metrics parser.

Observed against a server that answers with `Content-Encoding: zstd` while the flag is off:

```
enableZstd=false  ct="text/plain"  err=<nil>  out="(\xb5/\xfd\x04\x00\xb1\x00\x00metric_a 1\nmetric_b 2\nߨ\xb62"
enableZstd=true   ct="text/plain"  err=<nil>  out="metric_a 1\nmetric_b 2\n"
```

The scrape then fails inside the parser with `expected a valid start token, got "("`, which points at the metrics text rather than at the encoding. Prometheus only advertises `zstd` when the flag is on, so this needs a target or proxy that compresses regardless of `Accept-Encoding`, which RFC 9110 §12.5.3 forbids but is not rare.

Return an explicit error instead. This mirrors how the unified OTLP handler rejects a `Content-Encoding` it cannot decode (`storage/remote/codec.go`), and how the OpenMetrics 2.0 content type is rejected when its feature flag is off (`model/textparse/interface.go`).

Out of scope: the `switch` still passes any other unknown `Content-Encoding` through undecoded. That predates zstd support, and rejecting it would break targets that send a bogus header with an uncompressed body, so it is left alone.

Introduced in [#19502](https://redirect.github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/19502).

```release-notes
NONE
```

title: cmd/prometheus: default external URL scheme to https when web.config.file enables TLS
body:
Fixes #17236

```release-notes
[BUGFIX] Default --web.external-url to https when --web.config.file enables TLS.
```

## Problem

`computeExternalURL` (`cmd/prometheus/main.go`) always infers `http://` as the scheme when `--web.external-url` is unset, regardless of whether `--web.config.file` actually configures TLS via `tls_server_config`. Alertmanager/UI links therefore show `http://` even when Prometheus is only serving HTTPS.

## Fix

Only inside the branch that builds the *inferred-default* URL (`u == ""`), check whether the web config file (if any) contains a `tls_server_config` key via a light YAML unmarshal, and use `https` as the scheme in that case. An explicitly-provided `--web.external-url` is never touched.

## Relation to #17272

A prior PR (#17272) attempted this exact fix and got real review from @bboreham, who correctly pointed out that merely checking whether `--web.config.file` is set isn't enough (the file can configure things other than TLS, e.g. basic auth only) — the fix needs to specifically check for `tls_server_config`. That PR's author addressed the feedback but the PR stalled without further review and was self-closed. This PR follows the same validated approach (light YAML unmarshal, check `tls_server_config` presence, `go.yaml.in/yaml/v2` — already a direct dependency, no new dependency added) but with one correction: #17272 applied the scheme override unconditionally after `url.Parse`, for *any* `u` — which would silently override an explicitly user-supplied `--web.external-url`'s scheme too (e.g. an explicit `https://...` with no matching web-config file would get forced back to `http`). This PR only computes the scheme while building the synthetic default URL, so an explicit `--web.external-url` is left exactly as given — see `TestComputeExternalURLExplicitSchemeUnaffectedByWebConfig`.

## Testing

- `go vet ./cmd/prometheus/...` — clean.
- `gofmt -l` on changed files — clean.
- `go test ./cmd/prometheus/... -run 'TestComputeExternalURL' -v` — all pass, including the existing `TestComputeExternalURL` (updated for the new parameter) and two new tests: `TestComputeExternalURLWithWebConfig` (no config / TLS config / basic-auth-only config / nonexistent file) and `TestComputeExternalURLExplicitSchemeUnaffectedByWebConfig`.
- Full `go test ./cmd/prometheus/...` — passes, no regressions (~37s).
- Confirmed the new tests actually exercise the fix: temporarily neutered `webConfigHasTLSServerConfig` to always return `false` and confirmed the TLS-config subtest fails as expected (`expected: https, actual: http`), then restored the fix and reconfirmed all green.
- `golangci-lint run ./cmd/prometheus/...` (installed the exact pinned `v2.11.4` per `Makefile.common`) — clean. CI's first run caught one real finding (`interface{}` should be `any`, the `modernize` linter) before this was installed locally; fixed and reconfirmed clean.

Prometheus allows runtime configuration reloads. When `prometheus.yaml` is modified and a reload is invoked, Prometheus applies the new settings. The Prometheus Operator utilizes a `config-reloader` sidecar to manage this process.

### Real usecase
Custom `config-reloader` works by unmarshaling the default `prometheus.yaml` into a `Config` struct, appending `RemoteReadConfig`, and marshaling it back into YAML.

This PR removes the `,omitempty` tag from the `FilterExternalLabels` field.
* **Safe:** This is a non-breaking change.
* **Isolated:** The field will only explicitly appear in configurations that actively use `RemoteReadConfig`.

title: storage: make AppenderV2.AppendExemplars mandatory, drop it from Append
body:
TL;DR; Exemplars are not associated with samples in a pull model on a conceptual level. When we scrape a sample at timestamp T, the exemplar scraped at the same time might have timestamp T-3h or whatever.

I'm testing if making this change makes AppenderV2 easier to adopt in RW1, RW2. See #19250, #19251, #19252 without this change.

## Summary

`AppenderV2.Append` currently accepts exemplars inline via `AppendV2Options.Exemplars`, which means every implementation also has to carry the `AppendPartialError` plumbing needed to report per-exemplar failures out of a call whose primary job is appending one sample.

This moves exemplars to their own mandatory method on `AppenderV2`:

```go
AppendExemplars(ref SeriesRef, ls labels.Labels, exemplars []exemplar.Exemplar) (SeriesRef, error)
```

mirroring how `AppenderV1` already separates `AppendExemplar` from `Append`, but keeping it **batched** (a slice, not one exemplar at a time) so the scrape hot path doesn't regress to one extra interface call per exemplar.

Making it mandatory (rather than an optional capability interface with a runtime type-assertion) removes the need for that capability-check plumbing entirely — every `AppenderV2` implementation must support it, same as V1's `AppendExemplar`.

## Changes

- `storage/interface_append.go`: add `AppendExemplars` to `AppenderV2`, drop `Exemplars` from `AppendV2Options`, retarget `AppendPartialError`'s docs from `Append` to `AppendExemplars`.
- `tsdb/head_append_v2.go`, `tsdb/agent/db_append_v2.go`: implement `AppendExemplars`, drop exemplar handling from `Append`.
- `storage/fanout.go`: dispatch `AppendExemplars` to primary + secondaries (same pattern `Append` used for exemplar partial errors before).
- `scrape/scrape_append_v2.go` + `scrape/scrape.go`: call `AppendExemplars` after a successful `Append`; split the old `checkAddError`'s exemplar-partial-error branch into its own `checkExemplarsAddError`.
- `storage/remote/otlptranslator/prometheusremotewrite/{helper,histograms,number_data_points}.go`: attach exemplars via `AppendExemplars` after `Append` instead of inline (including the histogram-bucket exemplar-distribution loop in `helper.go`).
- `storage/remote/write_otlp_handler.go`: move the partial-error-hiding logic from the `Append` wrapper to a new `AppendExemplars` wrapper.
- `storage/remote/write.go`: `timestampTrackerV2` counts exemplars via `AppendExemplars` instead of `opts.Exemplars`.
- `cmd/prometheus/main.go`: `notReadyAppenderV2` gets an `AppendExemplars` stub.

title: tsdb: add conflicting-samples counter for commit-time series collisions
body:
Fixes #11725.

## Problem

When metric relabeling collapses two distinct series onto one, both samples pass `Append` (the batch `maxTime` is still stale because the batch is uncommitted). The conflict is only detected at `Commit`, where `series.appendable` returns an `ErrDuplicateSampleForTimestamp`-family error. That error fell into the bare `default` branch of `handleAppendableError`, which decremented the appended count with no counter and no log, so the losing sample vanished with no signal at all (the scrape-level duplicate warning only fires for `Append`-time errors, never for this commit-only path).

## Fix

Add `prometheus_tsdb_conflicting_samples_total{type=...}`, incremented per `ErrDuplicateSampleForTimestamp` rejection in `handleAppendableError`, flushed once per `Commit` via the same accumulate-int-then-`Add` pattern the existing out-of-order / out-of-bound / too-old reject counters already use. New `head_test.go` unit test on `AppenderV2` asserts the counter increments when two same-timestamp different-value samples for one series are committed together.

## Notes for review

- **V2 + performance.** Per the discussion (V2 is enough, perf is critical) the change is in the commit path that `AppenderV2` uses. There is no separate v2 `Commit`: both appenders embed `headAppenderBase`, so the counter also covers v1. That is purely additive observability with no behavior change (v1 already dropped these samples), but flagging it since the diff is not in a v2-only file.
- **Allocation-proven.** `storage.ErrDuplicateSampleForTimestamp` is a value-typed sentinel, so passing it straight to `errors.Is` in the per-sample path heap-boxes it on every call. It is pre-boxed once into an `error` interface (`errConflictingSample`) to avoid that. `benchstat` over `BenchmarkHeadAppender_AppendCommit/appender=v2` (`-count 10`) shows **zero allocs/op delta** across the matrix after this; the naive version regressed the histogram+exemplar cases by ~6-8% allocs/op, which the pre-boxing removes.
- **Counter-only, by design.** No per-sample log: under this exact failure mode a log would reintroduce unbounded hot-path cost. The counter is the observability the issue asks for.
- **Metric name.** I used `prometheus_tsdb_conflicting_samples_total` to match the existing reject-counter family (`prometheus_tsdb_out_of_order_samples_total`, etc.). The issue thread also floated `prometheus_tsdb_conflicting_samples_for_timestamp_total`; happy to rename if you prefer that spelling.

Signed-off-by present (DCO).

```release-notes
[ENHANCEMENT] TSDB: Add `prometheus_tsdb_conflicting_samples_total` metric counting samples rejected at commit because another sample with the same timestamp but a different value already existed for the series.
```

title: tsdb: recover from checkpoint corruption without truncating valid WAL
body:
## Problem

When replaying a corrupted checkpoint during `tsdb.Open`, `head.Init` previously returned a generic error wrapping `wlog.CorruptionErr`. The caller in `tsdb.Open` caught this error and invoked `wal.Repair` against the main WAL directory. Because the checkpoint segment index (e.g. `0`) did not correspond to segment indices in the main WAL directory, `wal.Repair` mistakenly truncated or wiped all segments in the healthy main WAL, resulting in complete data loss for all post-checkpoint samples.

## Solution

1. Introduced `errLoadCheckpoint` in `tsdb/head_wal.go` to explicitly distinguish checkpoint replay errors from WAL replay errors.
2. In `tsdb/head.go`, wrapped checkpoint loading errors in `&errLoadCheckpoint{checkpointDir: dir, err: err}`.
3. In `tsdb/db.go`, on encountering an `errLoadCheckpoint`, `tsdb.Open` safely removes the corrupted checkpoint directory and re-runs `head.Init` to replay the remaining un-corrupted WAL segments from `minValidTime`, preserving all post-checkpoint data.
4. Added `TestCheckpointCorruptionRecovery` in `tsdb/db_test.go` to verify corrupted checkpoint cleanup and successful replay of subsequent WAL records.

#### Which issue(s) does the PR fix:
Fixes #7530


title: Kubernetes SD discovery selectors do not work as expected
body:
### What did you do?

I want to deploy an OTEL agent (specifically [ADOT](https://github.com/aws-observability/aws-otel-collector) that uses Prometheus discovery in a DaemonSet mode on Kubernetes. My use-case is monitoring of Kubernetes data plane components (kubelet, cAdvisor, node-exporter, cni, kube-proxy, etc - mostly other daemonSets) in a huge cluster (3-5K nodes). To optimise collector performance I want to use `selectors` to filter out everything that is not on a particular node. According to [documentation](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/tree/main/discovery#other-implementation-considerations) it is a way to improve performance:
> SDs are intended to dump all possible targets. ... For large deployments where you are only interested in a small proportion of the returned targets, this may cause performance issues. If this occurs it is acceptable to also offer filtering via whatever mechanisms the SD exposes. ... Keep in mind that this is a performance optimisation, it should be possible to do the same filtering using relabelling alone. As with SD generally, we do not invent new ways to filter targets (that is what relabelling is for), merely offer up whatever functionality the SD itself offers.

Without it, collectors start consuming a lot of memory and CPU on each node, keeping a copy of all pods/nodes/etc on each DS instance. 

Kubernetes service discovery documentation says that:
> The endpoints role supports pod, service and endpoints selectors. The **pod role supports node selectors** when configured with `attach_metadata: {node: true}`.

Based on that I expect that I can use selector with node name to discover only pods on the node:
```yaml
- job_name: kubernetes-local-pods
  kubernetes_sd_configs:
    - role: pod
      attach_metadata:
        node: true
      selectors:
         - role: node
          label: "kubernetes.io/hostname=$K8S_NODE_NAME=$K8S_NODE_NAME"
```


### What did you expect to see?

I expect that by filtering out PODs by node name or IP i can drastically improve performance of each collector.

### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances?

However, pod role *doesn't* really support node's selector:
```
* error decoding 'receivers': error reading configuration for "prometheus": prometheus receiver failed to unmarshal yaml to prometheus config: pod role supports only pod selectors
```

title: Metrics for service discovery latency/age of discovered targets
body:
### Proposal

We are monitoring hundreds of Kubernetes clusters from some central observability clusters. To decide whether a cluster is operating fine, relying on current service discovery information seems a reasonable idea -- if we cannot update service discovery information, we definitely have issues with this cluster.

Currently, there are no reasonably usable metrics for this. As we're monitoring across the network, _some_ HTTP errors during service discovery are kind of expected, and just indicate issues after all -- for Prometheus service discovery, we don't mind some errors, but care about whether service discovery works _often enough_ to have a current state. So monitoring based on `prometheus_sd_kubernetes_http_request_total` doesn't work out too well.

There is also `prometheus_sd_updates_total`, but on one hand this is aggregated over all service discovery targets (and a rate still going up even if API server is down), on the other hand it's also just a kind of indirect observation.

I could well imagine all kinds of service discovery should be able to provide a timestamp of the last service discovery update, so a generic alert on failing service discovery for 15 minutes is as easy as `time() - prometheus_sd_last_update > 300`. This metric should be _per service discovery_ configuration block. From a very first peak at the code, this might easily be implemented centrally in `discovery/manager.go` in the update handling code.
